messages.subject: Update on Discrete Choice Modelling with Stan
parts:
HI All

I have been reporting here about a Discrete Choice Modelling analysis (using Hierarchical Bayes approach) I have been working on and a number of you have helped me as a first time user of Stan. It appears I have hit a dead end of sorts in terms of my model and I think this is because of deficiencies in my application and model. Any help would be fantastic. Here are some of my observations:

1. Model accuracy: The model predicts with only a 36% accuracy. With 3 choices to predict, the baseline is 33%. So 36% s nothing to write about

2. When I took the average of the parameters (posterior distributions), I noticed something peculiar: all of the parameters are converging around a very similar neighbhorhood of a point estimate value (between 0.05 and 0.07; never seen this happen before and it tells me that my model specification is not working. See below


0.066763 0.059144 0.061299 0.06701 0.052602 0.056744 0.060316 0.05978 0.065653
a12 a22 a23 a32 a33 a42 a43 a52 a53
 
I have five categorical predictors (a1 has two levels, a2 to a5 have three levels each) and hence 9 individual level betas that are estimated.

Per respondent I have 8 tasks, 3 choice in each task (there is no "none" option). If a profile (indicated by stim) was chosen, then it is coded as a 1 on that line.

Thanks

I don't see any immediate problems with the models. Do all the parameters
wind up with R-hat values very close to 1?

Usually, you want to do prediction in the generated quantities block if
you're using full Bayes. The problem may be in off-by-one in some extraction
part of the code.

You may also want to trace that the data's getting in properly. Do
you have a simpler model to try to make sure the data's OK?

- Bob

messages.author: cd58faac69dbf2d8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Update on Discrete Choice Modelling with Stan
parts:
Hey Krishna,

„choice" in your Dataset is a boolean which is TRUE for the chosen alternative and false otherwise. However, as Bob said „Categorical outcomes are numbered 1:K in Stan if there are K
outcomes.“ Hence, your dependent variable is the number of the chosen alternative in each choice set.

I must admit that my comment in the Stan code int<lower=1,upper=J> y[N]; // alternative selected is not super informative. But you see, y in an interger between 1 and J (number of alternative for each choice set) and you have N observations, which is the number of choice sets.

Hope this helps.

Best,
Daniel
